title: Coding 3D Models Is Easier Than You Think! #OpenSCAD
description:
Welcome to my quick introduction to OpenSCAD — a powerful 3D modeling program that combines coding and 3D design! In this video, I show you the basics of creating 3D and 2D objects, using transformations like translate, rotate, and scale, and working with Boolean operations like union, difference, and intersection.

You’ll also see how to highlight objects, use parametric models, and customize designs from Thingiverse. Whether you’re a beginner or just curious about OpenSCAD, this video will help you get started with coding your own 3D models.

If you enjoy this video, don’t forget to like, subscribe, and hit the bell for more 3D modeling tutorials!

Download Links / Resources:
 • OpenSCAD: https://www.openscad.org
 • Thingiverse: https://www.thingiverse.com

title: Hearing The Click Of A 5 Volt Relay Switch REK-11 РЕК11
description:
Relay REK-11 is a hermetically sealed electromagnetic relay designed for switching DC and AC circuits (up to 10 kHz). It is widely used in aviation, aerospace, and military equipment due to its high reliability and resistance to extreme conditions.
Key Specifications

    Relay Type:

        Two-position, single-stable (self-resetting).

        2 changeover (SPDT) contacts.

        Hermetic housing (protection against moisture, dust, and vibration).

    Electrical Parameters:

        Coil Voltage:

            YAL4.550.005: 27 V ±5% (standard version).

            YAL4.550.005-01: 12 V ±10%.

            YAL4.550.005-02: 6 V ±10%.

        Coil Resistance:

            1650 Ω (27 V), 420 Ω (12 V), 105 Ω (6 V).

        Operating Current:

            From 9 mA (27 V) to 32.6 mA (6 V).

        Switching Time: 1–5 ms.

    Switching Capabilities:

        Max. Current: Up to 3 A (resistive load).

        Open-Contact Voltage: Up to 34 V.

        Lifespan:

            500,000 cycles (low-current loads).

            25,000 cycles (inductive loads).

    Operating Conditions:

        Temperature Range: –60°C to +125°C.

        Humidity: Up to 98% at +35°C.

        Vibration Resistance: Up to 5000 Hz (300 m/s² acceleration).

        Shock Resistance: Up to 5000 m/s² (short-term).

    Service Life:

        15 years (when stored in a heated facility).

        Reduced under harsh conditions (see coefficient table).

Construction & Wiring

    Contact Groups:

        11, 12, 13 – First group (COM, NO, NC).

        21, 22, 23 – Second group (COM, NO, NC).

    Contact Material: P-1 alloy with gold plating (Zl1tv).

    Contact Resistance: ≤ 0.25 Ω.

title: Display your youtube follower count with #arduino #tm1637
description:
Here’s a detailed description for a project that uses a TM1637-based 4-digit 7-segment display with an Arduino R4 (with Wi-Fi capabilities) to fetch and display a YouTube subscriber count using the Google API:

In this project, I’ll show you how to create a real-time YouTube subscriber counter using an Arduino R4 with Wi-Fi, a TM1637 4-digit 7-segment display, and the Google API. This setup is ideal for tracking your YouTube channel’s subscriber growth in real time, making it perfect for YouTubers, content creators, and electronics enthusiasts interested in IoT projects.

The Arduino R4’s built-in Wi-Fi capabilities allow us to connect directly to the internet, where we can access Google’s YouTube Data API to fetch subscriber count data. The TM1637 display is compact, power-efficient, and easy to integrate, making it a great choice for this project to show dynamic data in a simple, visible way.

Project Overview

With the YouTube Data API and a little code, we can retrieve the current subscriber count for any YouTube channel. The Arduino R4 will connect to Wi-Fi, use the Google API to query the subscriber data, and then update the TM1637 display with the current count. I’ll walk you through each step, from setting up the API credentials to coding the Arduino and wiring up the display.

What You’ll Learn

 1. How to set up the Google API Console to obtain API keys and authorize your Arduino to access YouTube channel data.
 2. Programming the Arduino R4 with Wi-Fi to connect to your Wi-Fi network and query the YouTube Data API.
 3. Integrating the TM1637 4-digit 7-segment display with Arduino to display numbers in a clear, compact format.
 4. Coding the Arduino to fetch data, parse the response, and update the display.

Key Components:

 • Arduino R4 Wi-Fi: A powerful microcontroller with built-in Wi-Fi capability, making it perfect for IoT projects and web-based data applications.
 • TM1637 4-Digit 7-Segment Display: A simple, bright display used to show numbers clearly, ideal for presenting subscriber counts.
 • YouTube Data API: An API provided by Google that allows us to fetch YouTube channel metrics, including subscriber count.

Steps:

 1. Setup the YouTube Data API: Register your project on the Google API Console, enable the YouTube Data API, and generate API keys for access.
 2. Programming the Arduino R4: Write code to connect to Wi-Fi, send HTTP requests to the YouTube API, and retrieve subscriber count data.
 3. Displaying the Subscriber Count: Use the TM1637 library to display the count on the 4-digit 7-segment display, updating it periodically.

Sample Applications

 • YouTube Subscriber Display: Place this counter on your desk or shelf to keep track of your subscribers as they grow!
 • Real-Time Metrics Display: Modify the code to fetch other YouTube metrics, such as view count or video count.
 • IoT Projects: This project can be adapted to show other real-time data by changing the API endpoint.

Challenges and Tips

 • API Limits: Be mindful of the request limits for the YouTube Data API to avoid exceeding the daily quota.
 • Error Handling: Implement error handling to reconnect if Wi-Fi is lost or if there are issues with the API response.
 • Display Constraints: The 4-digit display can only show four digits, so if your subscriber count is in the thousands, you’ll need to handle this by displaying only the last 4 digits, scrolling, or flashing the display for larger numbers.

With this setup, you’ll have a live YouTube subscriber counter that updates periodically to reflect changes in real-time! This project combines IoT, API usage, and Arduino programming to create a useful display that’s easy to customize. Make sure to like, subscribe, and hit the notification bell if you found this project interesting, and stay tuned for more fun with Arduino and IoT!

title: Want Accurate Measurements? Try This Little Module Now HX711
description:
To display readings from the HX711 on an I2C LCD using an Arduino Uno, you'll need to set up your code to initialize both the HX711 and the LCD, read data from the HX711, and then print that data to the LCD. Below is a complete example sketch for your setup:
Components Required:

    HX711
    Load Cell (connected to HX711)
    Arduino Uno
    I2C LCD (with PCF8574 module)

Wiring:

Your connections are already set up correctly as follows:

    HX711:
        VCC to 5V
        GND to GND
        SCK to D5
        DT to D6
    LCD_I2C:
        SDA to A4
        SCL to A5

Arduino Sketch:
https://gist.github.com/roboter/a097e4176e5e89a86056eea6906fdb0c

Explanation of the Code:

    Library Inclusions: We include the HX711 and LiquidCrystal_I2C libraries for interfacing with the HX711 load cell and the I2C LCD.
    Initialization: In the setup() function, we initialize the serial communication, LCD, and the HX711 scale.
    Taring: The scale.tare() function sets the current reading to 0, which is useful if you have a load on the scale.
    Reading Weight: In the loop() function, we continuously read the weight using scale.get_units(10), which averages 10 readings for better accuracy.
    Displaying Weight: We display the weight on the LCD and also print it to the serial monitor for debugging.

Additional Notes:

    Ensure that you have installed the necessary libraries (HX711 and LiquidCrystal_I2C) via the Arduino Library Manager.
    You may need to adjust the scale factor using scale.set_scale(scale_factor); if your readings are off. You can do this by weighing a known weight and adjusting the scale factor accordingly.
